title: Dragon and Tiger 龍虎図 (Ryūko zu)

image.credit: Photograph via Wikimedia Commons (Maruyama Ōkyo 円山応挙 - Dragon and Tiger 龍虎図 (Ryūko zu) - 2023.583.16a, b - Metropolitan Museum of Art.jpg)

source.label: Wikipedia: “Ōkyo's first major commission came in 1768 from Yūjō, abbot of a temple in Ōtsu called Enman'in”
Fenollosa: “the animal forms of dragons in violent motion”
Wikipedia: “Ōkyo founded the Maruyama school of painting”

work.text: Perhaps the most stupendous efforts of Okio are when he chooses to combine motives of landscape, storm cloud and the animal forms of dragons in violent motion. … The body of the dragon is as realistically modelled in drawn scales as an enormous lizard in bronze.

source.author: Ernest F. Fenollosa
source.title: Epochs of Chinese and Japanese Art, Vol. II

work.text: However, the dragons, according to art critics such as Paine, demonstrate a weakness; they are treated academically, thus losing their grand, legendary essence.
work.lead: A dissenting view, on dragons in a later Ōkyo screen:

moment.text: He is especially famous for his tigers, and painted them in his youth with a patient realism, though his opportunities for study from nature must have been exceedingly limited.
moment.lead: Binyon, on Ganku, Ōkyo's younger Kyoto rival:

source.author: Laurence Binyon
source.title: Painting in the Far East (2nd edition)

matters.text: The line is from a poem attributed to a Yuan dynasty poet, Yu Ruyu (dates unknown), and describes the sound of a fierce wind lashing the ground. Wind is associated with the roar of the tiger.
matters.lead: Cleveland's curators, on a tiger scroll in Ōkyo's manner:

matters.text: Paired, the dragon (rising with clouds and rain) and the tiger (roaring with the wind on earth) are one of East Asian painting's oldest themes: two complementary powers of nature, heaven and earth.
